30:000 words
4:00 left: proofread now. NEG → NOUN → VERB → SPELL → SENTENCE. Add no new ideas.

The 4-minute proofread: five scans, always in this order

Start at 26:00 on the clock, whatever state the essay is in. Each scan looks for one thing only, which is why it catches what a general reread misses.

  1. NEG: meaning first. In each claim sentence, check not · no · never · cannot · few/a few · hardly. Does the sentence say what your argument needs? One dropped not turns your evidence against you.
  2. NOUN. Stop at every noun. Is it countable? One or many? Then choose a/an, the or nothing. Uncountable nouns never take -s: evidence, research, advice, information, knowledge, feedback, equipment, progress, logic.
  3. VERB. Find each verb's real subject, skipping of …, who/that … and along with …. The verb takes -s only when that subject is one thing. Use the present tense for claims and the past only inside past examples.
  4. SPELL. Read backward, from the last sentence to the first, word by word. Watch the near-misses: than/then · its/it's · none/non- · sometimes/sometime · affect/effect · lose/loose · whether/weather · principle/principal · led/lead · from/form · and/an · of/off · to/too · their/there. No contractions.
  5. SENTENCE. One main clause per sentence unless and/but/so or a semicolon joins them. A comma before however or therefore makes a splice: use a period or semicolon. Delete …, etc. and and so on. Every sentence needs a subject and a finite verb.

The 30-minute plan

  • 0:00–2:00 Plan. Write your position in one sentence, with its condition. Then 2–3 reasons, one example per reason that a general reader knows, and where you will answer the specific instruction.
  • 2:00–26:00 Write 5 paragraphs, about 450–600 words. Intro: 3 sentences (frame, position, roadmap). Body: 2–3 paragraphs, each claim → reason → example → why it matters. One paragraph does what the instruction asks. Conclusion: 2 sentences.
  • 26:00–30:00 Proofread: the five scans. Start no new sentence after 26:00.

Take a position; don't hedge

A scientist's instinct is “it depends; more research is needed.” A rater reads that as no position. Qualify instead: one position plus the condition under which it holds.

  • “I largely agree: X holds when A but fails when B, and because A is the usual case, the claim stands as a general rule.”
  • “The recommendation makes sense only where …; elsewhere it would …”
  • “Although the second view captures something real, the first better explains …”

State the position in the intro and repeat it in the conclusion with the same key words.

The six instruction types and what each one demands

TypeThe task asks you to…So your essay must…
A When it holdsagree or disagree, considering when the statement might or might not holdname a case where it holds and a case where it fails, and say how they shape your position
B Recommendationjudge a recommendation by the circumstances in which following it would or would not helpdescribe specific situations of each kind, not just general pros and cons
C Challengesagree or disagree while answering the strongest objectionsstate the best opposing argument fairly, then answer it
D Two viewssay which of two views is closer to yoursdiscuss both views, then explain why one fits better
E Claim + reasonevaluate a claim and the reason given for itjudge the claim and the reason separately (a true claim can rest on a weak reason)
F Policytake a view on a policy by weighing its consequencestrace likely consequences, intended and unintended, and let them decide your position

These are paraphrases. The ETS wording differs; read the real instruction twice before you plan.

Vietnamese → English traps

  • “the” + a general noun: The education is → Education is. General plurals and uncountable nouns take no article.
  • Uncountable + -s: evidences, researches, advices, informations, feedbacks, equipments, logics. To count, write studies or pieces of evidence.
  • “have” for existence: In cities have many jobs → There are many jobs in cities.
  • Double subject: The government, it should → The government should.
  • Two connectors: Although costs rose, but / Because …, so: keep one.
  • Word form: economic (of the economy) vs economical (cheap) · historic (famous) vs historical (of the past) · success / succeed / successful.
  • Nationality: Vietnamese's economy → Vietnam's economy.
  • Noun vs verb: a follow-up / to follow up · a setup / to set up.
  • Prepositions: discuss about, emphasize on, mention about → no preposition · depend on · interested in · the reason for · result in.

Articles in four questions

  1. A name or a general idea? Most countries and cities take Ø (Vietnam, Hanoi), but write the United States, the Philippines, the Mekong. A general plural or an uncountable noun takes Ø: Vaccines save lives. Education matters.
  2. Does the reader know which one? If it was mentioned before, is obvious or unique, is a superlative or ordinal, or is pinned down by of … or that … after it, use the.
  3. Singular, countable, and the reader doesn't know which one? Use a/an.
  4. a or an? Go by sound, not spelling: an hour, an MRI, an NGO; a university, a one-time, a European.

Never leave a singular countable noun bare: Government should → The government should / Governments should.

Examples a rater can follow

  • One example per reason, drawn from history, science, business, education or everyday life.
  • Use at most one example from your own field, in plain words. Write antibiotic resistance, not AMR; write a global study of disease burden, not GBD.
  • A specific, checkable example beats a hypothetical one: name the place, the period and the result.
  • Make every number add up. Don't invent precise statistics; “roughly half” is safer than a fake 47.3%.
